The **National Supervisory Commission of the People's Republic of China** is the country's highest state supervisory and anti-corruption authority. It is [co-located](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Co-located_office "Co-located office") with the [Central Commission for Discipline Inspection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection "Central Commission for Discipline Inspection") of the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP).

The National Supervisory Commission was formed in 2018 by an [amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_amendment_to_the_Constitution_of_China "2018 amendment to the Constitution of China") to the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_China "Constitution of China") as the merger of the [Ministry of Supervision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Supervision "Ministry of Supervision"), the [National Bureau of Corruption Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Bureau_of_Corruption_Prevention "National Bureau of Corruption Prevention"), and the [Supreme People's Procuratorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Procuratorate "Supreme People's Procuratorate")'s General Administration of Anti-Corruption and Bribery. Its tasks include monitoring policy implementation, investigating official malfeasance, and deciding administrative sanctions among civil servants. The NSC's jurisdiction includes all public sector employees as well as village officials whether or not they are CCP members.

The Commission holds the same constitutional status as that of the [State Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Council_of_China "State Council of China"), of the [Supreme People's Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Court "Supreme People's Court"), and of the [Supreme People's Procuratorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Procuratorate "Supreme People's Procuratorate"). The National Supervisory Commission is co-located with the CCP's CCDI, the party's supreme supervisory and disciplinary body, and the NSC effectively functions as the CCDI's state arm.

The National Supervisory Commission was formed as part of a series of reforms to China's anti-corruption system during the first term of [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") as General Secretary of the Communist Party. The NSC roots originated from the imperial Chinese supervision system which originated in the [Qin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_dynasty "Qin dynasty") and [Han dynasties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty"). The system has been functioning for more than two thousand years. The names and structures of the supervisory offices may vary from one dynasty to another. However, they share the same values. For centuries, these offices aimed to uphold justice, enforce discipline and supervise government ethics. To achieve the goals, government officials periodically investigated, conducted visits and reported cases of impeachment to emperors.

After the [1911 Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_Revolution "1911 Revolution"), the founder of the Republic of China, [Sun Yat-sen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Yat-sen "Sun Yat-sen") advocated a five-power constitution. Drawing from the Western separation of powers (three branches: a legislature, an executive, and a judiciary), he added another two traditional Chinese government powers, examination and supervision (control), to propose the Five-Power Constitution.[[1]](#cite_note-1) The [Constitution of the Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Republic_of_China "Constitution of the Republic of China") was promulgated in 1947 which made the [Control Yuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_Yuan "Control Yuan") a parliamentary chamber until the reforms of 1991 which it became the sole auditory body in Taiwan.

While the Communist Party had institutionalized internal mechanisms for combating corruption in some form since its founding and the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949, it was apparent that it was largely ineffective at curbing systemic corruption, and otherwise had no legal basis, as the main organ tasked with combating corruption and malfeasance, the [Central Commission for Discipline Inspection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection "Central Commission for Discipline Inspection"), was a party organ, not a state one.[[2]](#cite_note-dengj-2)

Prior to Xi's [anti-corruption campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-corruption_campaign_under_Xi_Jinping "Anti-corruption campaign under Xi Jinping"), offenses were often prosecuted at the direction of local party authorities through their control of local Commissions for Discipline Inspection (CDIs) and procuratorial organs. While these authorities theoretically reported to their superior commissions at the next higher level of administration (i.e. the municipal organ would report to the provincial one, the provincial organ would report into the CCDI), in addition to answering to the local party leadership, in reality the local CDIs only answered to local party leaders, as they controlled the budgets, personnel, and resources of these organizations. This often led to arbitrary exercise of power and political selectiveness in the targets of corruption efforts.[[2]](#cite_note-dengj-2)

In late 2016, pilot initiatives of the Supervisory Commissions (SCs) began in [Shanxi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanxi_Provincial_Supervisory_Commission "Shanxi Provincial Supervisory Commission"), [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Municipal_Supervisory_Commission "Beijing Municipal Supervisory Commission") and [Zhejiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhejiang_Provincial_Supervisory_Commission "Zhejiang Provincial Supervisory Commission"). Provincial level chiefs of Discipline Inspection began serving concurrently as heads of the local Supervisory Commissions.[[2]](#cite_note-dengj-2)

In February 2018, an [amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_amendment_to_the_Constitution_of_China "2018 amendment to the Constitution of China") to the [constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_China "Constitution of China") was proposed to make national and local supervision commissions official state organs. Local commissions will be appointed by local peoples' congresses at county and higher level and will be accountable to them and to the supervision commission at the higher level.[[3]](#cite_note-3) The amendment was passed on 11 March 2018 and went into effect on the same date.

On 17 March 2018, three state agencies with inspection powers (the [Ministry of Supervision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Supervision "Ministry of Supervision"), the [National Bureau of Corruption Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Bureau_of_Corruption_Prevention "National Bureau of Corruption Prevention"), and the [Supreme People's Procuratorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Procuratorate "Supreme People's Procuratorate")'s General Administration of Anti-Corruption and Bribery) were merged to form the new National Supervisory Commission.[[4]](#cite_note-:Tsang&Cheung-4): 57 The formation of the National Supervisory Commission centralized control of anti-corruption resources to the central authorities and was aimed at curbing local interference in anti-corruption efforts.[[2]](#cite_note-dengj-2)

The **Central Commission for Discipline Inspection** (**CCDI**)[[note 1]](#cite_note-1) is the supreme supervisory organ of the [Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP). The CCDI is elected and supervised by the [CCP National Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party"). It is tasked with defending the [party constitution](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Constitution of the Chinese Communist Party"), enforcing inner-party regulations, coordinating anti-corruption work, and safeguarding the core position of the [CCP general secretary](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") and the party as a whole. Safeguarding the political position of Xi and the Central Committee is, officially, the CCDI's highest responsibility. Since the vast majority of officials at all levels of government are also CCP members, the commission is, in practice, the top anti-corruption body in the [People's Republic of China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC).

At its first plenary session after being elected by a [CCP National Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party"), the CCDI elect its [secretary](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_the_Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection "Secretary of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection"), [deputy secretaries](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Secretary_of_the_Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection "Deputy Secretary of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection"), [secretary general](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_General_of_the_Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection "Secretary General of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection") and other [Standing Committee](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_Committee_of_the_Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection "Standing Committee of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection") members. The CCDI then reports the election results to the Central Committee, which can either approve or disapprove of the results. The CCDI Standing Committee is responsible for convening and presiding over plenary sessions of the CCDI. When the CCDI is not in session, its powers and responsibilities are delegated to the CCDI Standing Committee, which has to implement the decisions of the CCP Central Committee and the CCDI plenary sessions. It is held accountable to the CCDI plenary sessions. The secretary convenes, presides over the work and sets the agenda of the CCDI Standing Committee meetings. The current secretary is [Li Xi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Xi_(politician) "Li Xi (politician)"), who was elected by the 1st Plenary Session of the [20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection "20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection") and approved by the [20th Central Committee](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party") on 23 October 2022.[[1]](#cite_note-2)

The modern commission was established at the [3rd Plenary Session](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_Plenary_Session_of_the_11th_Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "3rd Plenary Session of the 11th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party") of the [11th Central Committee](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11th_Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "11th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party") in December 1978. The **People's Police** ([Chinese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 人民警察; [pinyin](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Rénmín Jǐngchá*) is the national [civilian police](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilian_police "Civilian police") force of the [People's Republic of China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China").[[1]](#cite_note-Sun2009-1): 120 It is led by the [Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP).

The People's Police include the People's Police of Public Security Organs, the People's Police of State Security Organs, the People's Police of Judicial Administration Organs, the Judicial Police of People's Courts, and the Judicial Police of People's Procuratorates. The [Ministry of Public Security](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Public_Security_(China) "Ministry of Public Security (China)"), the [Ministry of State Security](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_State_Security_(China) "Ministry of State Security (China)"), the [Ministry of Justice](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Justice_(China) "Ministry of Justice (China)"), the [Supreme People's Court](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Court "Supreme People's Court"), and the [Supreme People's Procuratorate](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Procuratorate "Supreme People's Procuratorate") are the highest leadership and command organs of the above-mentioned categories of People's Police, and all of them are under the leadership of the CCP's [Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Political_and_Legal_Affairs_Commission "Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission"). The [People's Armed Police](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Armed_Police "People's Armed Police"), which is led and managed by the [Central Military Commission](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Military_Commission_(China) "Central Military Commission (China)"), is part of the national armed forces and does not belong to the People's Police.

Police in China have a variety of roles in addition to enforcing the law.

They are also responsible for the maintenance of social stability (维护社会稳定; *Wéihù Shèhùi Wěndìng*), and in this sense perform not just a law enforcement function but a political function as well. The majority of national police forces are under the jurisdiction of the [Ministry of Public Security](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Public_Security_(China) "Ministry of Public Security (China)") (MPS).

Over the years, the power of the police has gradually been expanded to border control, under the auspices of the [National Immigration Administration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Immigration_Administration "National Immigration Administration") (NIA), household registration, issuance of the [National ID card](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_document "Identity document") (see: [Resident Identity Card](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resident_Identity_Card "Resident Identity Card")) and cybersecurity (under the 11th Bureau of the MPS), network security and website registration.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

In the PRC, *People's Police* refers to the identity of [law enforcement officers](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_enforcement_officer "Law enforcement officer"),[[3]](#cite_note-3) while *Public Security* or *the* *police* denotes a specific government agency, namely the [*public security organs*](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_security_bureau_(China) "Public security bureau (China)").[[4]](#cite_note-4) Although prison police, judicial police, and other such units also fall under the police system, due to the special nature of their work, they are generally not referred to as *the* *police*.

Before the turn of the 21st century, public security officers often used *Public Security* as their designation and term of address, rather than the broader term *the* *police*. Additionally, public security officers, who handle the majority of public order and criminal cases, are the most frequently encountered police force by the public. These factors have led some people, especially those in [Hong Kong](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong"), [Taiwan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan"), and [overseas Chinese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overseas_Chinese "Overseas Chinese") communities, to inaccurately refer to mainland China's police officers as *Public Security.[[5]](#cite_note-5)*

The [uniforms](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform "Uniform") and [vehicle](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle "Vehicle") liveries of the People's Police generally maintain a consistent style, with their primary distinctions being the inscriptions indicating the departments to which various police forces belong, namely *Public Security*, *Justice*, *State Security*, *Court*, and *Procuratorate*.

Founded in October 1949 with the inception of the [People's Republic of China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), and controlled by the [Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP), China's major national police force operates under the Ministry of Public Security (MPS).[[6]](#cite_note-comparative-6)

The influence of the [Soviet Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") was paramount in the early years of the People's Republic, and guided the Chinese approach to policing.

During the [Cultural Revolution](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution") (1966–76), the powers of the police were both strengthened and weakened; on the one hand, they were given control over much of the judicial system, since [People's Courts](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Court "Supreme People's Court") and [People's Procuratorates](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Procuratorate "Supreme People's Procuratorate") basically collapsed, meaning that local directors of public security bureaus could easily arrest and convict almost any person they chose; on the other hand, the top leadership of the police was almost totally purged and persecuted, and [political commissars](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_commissar "Political commissar") from the PLA (most of them hand-picked by the [Cultural Revolution Group](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution_Group "Cultural Revolution Group")) were brought in to take control over the largest and most important public security bureaus, including those of [Beijing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing") and [Shanghai](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai").[[6]](#cite_note-comparati

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterterrorism_in_China:
**Terrorism in the People's Republic of China** encompasses the employment of [violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violence "Violence") or threats thereof to instigate political or ideological shifts within the country. The [Chinese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") identifies terrorism as one of the "[Three Evils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Evils "Three Evils")," alongside [separatism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separatism "Separatism") and [religious extremism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_fanaticism "Religious fanaticism"), viewing these as interconnected threats to [national security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_security "National security") and social stability.[[1]](#cite_note-britannica-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) These forces are seen by [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing") as interconnected threats to social stability and national security. In particular, terrorism is viewed as a violent manifestation of [ethnic separatism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separatism "Separatism"), and separatism is understood as a corollary of religious [zealotry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealots "Zealots").[[3]](#cite_note-Chung-3) The government has embarked on [strike-hard campaigns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_Hard_Campaign_Against_Violent_Terrorism "Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism") to suppress these tendencies, particularly in the [Muslim majority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_Hard_Campaign_against_Violent_Terrorism "Strike Hard Campaign against Violent Terrorism") [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang") and the [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist "Buddhist") [Tibetan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet_Autonomous_Region "Tibet Autonomous Region") provinces.[[3]](#cite_note-Chung-3)

Following the [9/11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks") in 2001, the PRC strengthened its involvement in multilateral and bilateral [counterterrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-terrorism "Counter-terrorism") efforts. As a result, several [Uyghur separatist movements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Turkestan_independence_movement "East Turkestan independence movement") have been labelled as terrorist groups by the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") and the [U.S. Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State").[[4]](#cite_note-4) There have been allegations that the [Chinese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") has been applying charges of terrorism in an inconsistent and politically motivated manner.[[5]](#cite_note-Wayne-5) These represent one of the contributing factors that play into the existing [tensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Uyghurs_in_China "Persecution of Uyghurs in China") between the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") and the [Uyghur minority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs").

On the 23rd of January 2024, the [Information Office of the State Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Council_Information_Office "State Council Information Office") released a [white paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_paper "White paper") on "[China's Counter-Terrorism Legal System and Practice](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/%E4%B8%AD%E5%9B%BD%E7%9A%84%E5%8F%8D%E6%81%90%E6%80%96%E4%B8%BB%E4%B9%89%E6%B3%95%E5%BE%8B%E5%88%B6%E5%BA%A6%E4%BD%93%E7%B3%BB%E4%B8%8E%E5%AE%9E%E8%B7%B5 "s:中国的反恐怖主义法律制度体系与实践")," which emphasized that China is a victim of terrorism and continues to face it as a threat.[[6]](#cite_note-6) Subsequently, on the 24th of January, the [People's Daily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Daily "People's Daily") published an [opinion piece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opinion_piece "Opinion piece") demanding that anti-terrorism work must be carried out under the established legal systems.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

## Chinese cultural context

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Terrorism_in_China&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Chinese cultural context")]

While there is no international or legally binding [definition of terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Definitions_of_terrorism "Definitions of terrorism"), internationally recognized organizations such as the [UN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") and the [EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") have defined terrorism in various resolutions.[[8]](#cite_note-Martyn-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) In the cultural setting of China, the term is relatively new and ambiguous.[[10]](#cite_note-Eterno-10)

The concept of terrorism, as it evolved and is understood in the West, did not exist in [Imperial China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_China#Imperial_China "History of China"). There, [political crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_crime "Political crime") took the form of [violence against the emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regicide "Regicide"), and was viewed as harmful as it induced fear and led to "chaos".[[10]](#cite_note-Eterno-10) With the exception of "good" [political violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_violence "Political violence") against rulers whose lack of [propriety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propriety "Propriety") and [virtue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtue "Virtue") resulted in loss of the [Mandate of heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandate_of_heaven "Mandate of heaven"), violence was seen as contrary to human nature and the [Tao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tao "Tao").[[10]](#cite_note-Eterno-10) Kam Wong argues that the dynamics of imperial China form the basis for contemporary Chinese understandings of terrorism.[[10]](#cite_note-Eterno-10)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/May_2014_%C3%9Cr%C3%BCmqi_attack-VOA_01.jpg/250px-May_2014_%C3%9Cr%C3%BCmqi_attack-VOA_01.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:May_2014_%C3%9Cr%C3%BCmqi_attack-VOA_01.jpg)

Soldiers guard the entrance to the scene of the [May 2014 Urumqi attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_2014_%C3%9Cr%C3%BCmqi_attack "May 2014 Ürümqi attack")

Fear of chaos and [social disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_disorder "Social disorder") is a powerful factor in mobilizing political will to combat potential threats.[[11]](#cite_note-Ogden-11)[[5]](#cite_note-Wayne-5) In the modern context, any group or force with the potential to challenge the existing social order or the [political security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_security "Political security") of the rulers may be considered a form of terrorism. It is "to be condemned unrelentingly and suppressed at all costs," according to Wong.[[10]](#cite_note-Eterno-10)

There is currently no clearly established definition for terrorism either nationally or internationally,[[12]](#cite_note-Amnesty-12) though the [National People's Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Congress "National People's Congress") is in the process of drafting legislation that would clarify the use of the term in [Chinese law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_law "Chinese law"). The draft legislation, as reported by [Xinhua News Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinhua_News_Agency "Xinhua News Agency"), classified as terrorist acts that "cause or aim to cause severe harm to society by causing casualties, bringing about major economic losses, damaging public facilities or disturbing social order."[[13]](#cite_note-BBC-13) [Human rights groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_group "Human rights group") charge that the term is sometimes applied to non-violent [dissidents in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Chinese_dissidents "List of Chinese dissidents").[[12]](#cite_note-Amnesty-12)[[14]](#cite_note-CECC2005-14)

## Regionally focused terrorism and political violence

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Terrorism_in_China&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Regionally focused terrorism and political violence")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Xinjiang_in_China_%28de-facto%29.svg/250px-Xinjiang_in_China_%28de-facto%29.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Xinjiang_in_China_(de-facto).svg)

Xinjiang, literally "new frontier," is a provincial-level autonomous region situated in the northwest of the People's Republic of China.

Media reports and scholarly studies of terrorism in contemporary China frequently focus on members of the largely Muslim [Uyghur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") [ethnic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnicity "Ethnicity"), who are concentrated in the northwestern province of [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang").[[11]](#cite_note-Ogden-11)

Throughout its history, the region now known as Xinjiang was ruled intermittently by China.[[15]](#cite_note-MAR-15) The Turkic Uyghurs generally identify more closely with the cultures of Central Asia and have historically resisted attempts at assimilation into [Han Chinese culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Chinese "Han Chinese").

From 1933 to 1934, Uyghurs founded a short-lived [Islamic republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_East_Turkestan_Republic "First East Turkestan Republic"), and the Soviets supported Communist Uyghur rebels in the [Ili Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ili_Rebellion "Ili Rebellion") from 1944 to 1949 against the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)") and the [Second East Turkestan Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_East_Turkestan_Republic "Second East Turkestan Republic"), before the [Incorporation of Xinjiang i

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Supreme_People%27s_Court_of_P.R.China%27s_badge.svg/250px-Supreme_People%27s_Court_of_P.R.China%27s_badge.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Supreme_People's_Court_of_P.R.China's_badge.svg)

Emblem of the People's Court of the People's Republic of China

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/More_China_040.JPG/250px-More_China_040.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:More_China_040.JPG)

The front facade of the [Supreme People's Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Court "Supreme People's Court") in Beijing.

The [judiciary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judiciary "Judiciary") of the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC) is organized under the principle of [unified state power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unified_state_power "Unified state power") of the [National People's Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Congress "National People's Congress") (NPC) and is represented by its two primary judicial organs, the [Supreme People's Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Court "Supreme People's Court") and the [Supreme People's Procuratorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Procuratorate "Supreme People's Procuratorate"). These organs are [constitutionally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_China "Constitution of China") inferior and accountable to the NPC as the [supreme state organ of power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_state_organ_of_power "Supreme state organ of power"), and implement its political will.

[Judicial independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_independence "Judicial independence") and [judicial review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_review "Judicial review") are nonexistent, as courts do not have power beyond what is granted to them by the NPC. The [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party")'s [Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Political_and_Legal_Affairs_Commission "Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission") maintains effective control over the court system and its personnel.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judiciary_of_Hong_Kong "Judiciary of Hong Kong") and [Macau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judiciary_of_Macau "Judiciary of Macau") have separate court systems in accordance with the "[one country, two systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_country,_two_systems "One country, two systems")" doctrine.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/VM_4660_Supreme_Court_of_Hubei_Province.jpg/250px-VM_4660_Supreme_Court_of_Hubei_Province.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:VM_4660_Supreme_Court_of_Hubei_Province.jpg)

High People's Court of the province of Hubei

According to the 1982 [state constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_China "Constitution of China") and the Organic Law of the People's Courts that went into effect on January 1, 1980, the Chinese courts are divided into a four-level court system (Supreme, High, Intermediate and Primary):

* The [Supreme People's Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_People's_Court "Supreme People's Court") (SPC) is the [supreme judicial organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_judicial_organ "Supreme judicial organ") of the state and is located in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), and acts as the premier appellate forum of the land and court of last resort, which supervises the administration of justice by all subordinate "local" and "special" people's courts. It also sets up six circuit courts seat outside of the state capital, which acts in the same capacity, to hear cross-provincial cases within respective jurisdiction.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]
* [Local people's courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_people's_court "Local people's court")—the courts of the first instance—handle [criminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_law "Criminal law") and [civil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_law_(common_law) "Civil law (common law)") cases. These people's courts make up the remaining three levels of the court system and consist of "[high people's courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_people's_court "High people's court")" at the level of the provinces, autonomous regions, and special municipalities; "[intermediate people's courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediate_people's_court "Intermediate people's court")" at the level of prefectures, autonomous prefectures, and municipalities; and "[primary people's courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_people's_court "Primary people's court")" at the level of autonomous counties, towns, and municipal districts.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]
* [Courts of Special Jurisdiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_special_jurisdiction_(People's_Republic_of_China) "Court of special jurisdiction (People's Republic of China)") (special courts) comprises the [Military Courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_court_(People's_Republic_of_China) "Military court (People's Republic of China)") (military), [Railway Transportation Court of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_Transportation_Court_(China)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Railway Transportation Court (China) (page does not exist)") (railroad transportation), [Maritime Courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_court_(People's_Republic_of_China) "Maritime court (People's Republic of China)") (water transportation), Internet Courts, Intellectual Property Courts, and Financial Court. Except for the Military Courts, all other courts of special jurisdiction falls under the general jurisdiction of its respective high court.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Candidates for judgeship must pass the [National Unified Legal Professional Qualification Examination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Unified_Legal_Professional_Qualification_Examination "National Unified Legal Professional Qualification Examination").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

The court system is paralleled by a hierarchy of prosecuting offices called people's procuratorates, the highest being the Supreme People's Procuratorate.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

As of 2012, all lawyers must take an oath pledging loyalty to the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party").[[3]](#cite_note-NYTOath-3) Local departments of justice can revoke the license of lawyers. This power is used to target lawyers who challenge the authority of the state, particularly human rights lawyers.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

The Supreme Court is responsible for establishing and monitoring legal procedures in adherence to the laws and orders made by the legislative organs.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Following civil law traditions, the courts do not establish legally-binding precedent. The Supreme Court has the right to publish legal explanations of laws which are legally-binding but the right to interpret the constitution is reserved by the [legislative organs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Congress "National People's Congress").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]
A verdict made by an inferior court can be challenged in its superior court, up to the Supreme Court, there are four levels of courts in total. A superior court can also designate any of its inferior courts to hear an appeal rather than do so itself.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Court proceedings in China are generally livestreamed, with exceptions including where classified information is discussed or where juveniles testify.[[5]](#cite_note-:9222-5): 125

Besides the court system, it is also encouraged to resolve civil conflicts through a state-sponsored and -regulated mediation and arbitration system. After the first hearing of a civil case, the court is required by law to ask both parties if they are willing to resolve their conflict through mediation. If agreed, the court should assign a mediator and oversee the process. If both parties reach an agreement, it will be legally binding after the agreement is reviewed and documented by a judge of the court.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Courts allow litigants to communicate with it via [WeChat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WeChat "WeChat"), through which the litigant parties can file lawsuits, participate in proceedings, present evidence, and listen to verdicts.[[5]](#cite_note-:9222-5): 125 As of December 2019, more than 3 million litigants had used WeChat for litigation.[[5]](#cite_note-:9222-5): 125

The [Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_Law_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China") is the code that stipulates crimes and criminal liability applicable in the country. Among them, the Criminal Law is a [basic law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_law "Basic law") of the People's Republic of China. Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-corruption_campaign_under_Xi_Jinping:
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/18th_National_Congress_of_the_Communist_Party_of_China.jpg/330px-18th_National_Congress_of_the_Communist_Party_of_China.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:18th_National_Congress_of_the_Communist_Party_of_China.jpg)

The anti-corruption campaign began after the conclusion of the [18th National Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "18th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party") of the [Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") held in Beijing in November 2012.



A far-reaching [anti-corruption](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-corruption "Anti-corruption") campaign was launched in [China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") following the conclusion of the [18th National Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "18th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party") of the [Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) in 2012. Initiated by [CCP general secretary](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping"), the campaign became the most extensive and systematic anti-corruption effort in the history of CCP governance. The campaign began with the [Central Commission for Discipline Inspection](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection "Central Commission for Discipline Inspection") (CCDI) conducting investigations and purging numerous high-ranking CCP and government officials, as well as [People's Liberation Army](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army "People's Liberation Army") (PLA) generals and heads of [state-owned enterprises](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-owned_enterprises_of_China "State-owned enterprises of China") and institutions, for violations of discipline and law. Nationwide, disciplinary inspection and supervision departments at all levels of the CCP and government have investigated and punished CCP members and senior officials for violations of discipline and law.

Upon assuming office, Xi pledged to crack down on both "tigers and flies", referring respectively to high-ranking officials and grassroots civil servants. Most of the officials investigated were dismissed from office and faced charges of bribery and [abuse of power](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abuse_of_power "Abuse of power"), though the severity and nature of the alleged misconduct varied considerably. Administered primarily by the CCDI its [Secretary](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_the_Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection "Secretary of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection") from 2012 to 2017, [Wang Qishan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Qishan "Wang Qishan"), alongside the relevant military and judicial bodies, the campaign has targeted hundreds of senior officials, including dozens of ministerial-level official and senior PLA officers, hundreds of deputy ministerial-level officials, several executives of [state-owned enterprises](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-owned_enterprises_of_China "State-owned enterprises of China"), and five national leaders. The campaign has also led to strengthening of the CCDI apparatus within the CCP, as well as enhanced power over local Discipline Inspection Commissions. In 2018, the [National Supervisory Commission](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Supervisory_Commission "National Supervisory Commission") was formed as the country's highest state supervisory body following a merger various anti-corruption government departments, strengthening the CCDI's powers and reach.

The campaign notably investigated both sitting and former national-level leaders. These included former [Politburo Standing Committee](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politburo_Standing_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party") (PSC) member [Zhou Yongkang](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Yongkang "Zhou Yongkang") and former Politburo members and [Central Military Commission](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Military_Commission_(China) "Central Military Commission (China)") (CMC) [vice chairmen](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Chairman_of_the_Central_Military_Commission "Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission") [Xu Caihou](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xu_Caihou "Xu Caihou") and [Guo Boxiong](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guo_Boxiong "Guo Boxiong"). The campaign also targeted sitting Politburo members such as Chongqing CCP committee secretary [Sun Zhengcai](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Zhengcai "Sun Zhengcai") in 2017, CMC vice chairmen [He Weidong](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He_Weidong "He Weidong") and [Zhang Youxia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Youxia "Zhang Youxia") in 2025 and 2026 respectively. and former [Xinjiang CCP committee secretary](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_Secretary_of_Xinjiang "Party Secretary of Xinjiang") [Ma Xingrui](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma_Xingrui "Ma Xingrui") in 2026. As of 2023, approximately 2.3 million government officials had been [prosecuted](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosecuted "Prosecuted"). The campaign formed a central component of a broader initiative aimed at curbing corruption within the CCP and reinforcing internal unity through a process termed [self-revolution](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-revolution "Self-revolution"). It has since become one of the defining features of Xi's political legacy and has been cited as a key factor that allowed Xi to consolidate power.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Wang_Qishan_in_2016.jpg/120px-Wang_Qishan_in_2016.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wang_Qishan_in_2016.jpg)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Ombudsman_sign.jpg/330px-Ombudsman_sign.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ombudsman_sign.jpg)

Sign in [Banjul](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banjul "Banjul"), capital of [The Gambia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gambia "The Gambia"), giving directions to the ombudsman's office

An **ombudsman** ( [*OM-buudz-mən*](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"), also [*-⁠bədz-, -⁠budz-*](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)) is a government official who investigates and tries to resolve complaints, usually through recommendations (binding or not) or [mediation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediation "Mediation"). They are usually appointed by the [government](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government "Government") or by [parliament](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament "Parliament") (often with a significant degree of independence).

Ombudsmen also aim to identify systemic issues leading to poor service or breaches of people's rights. At the national level, most ombudsmen have a wide mandate to deal with the entire public sector, and sometimes also elements of the private sector (for example, contracted service providers). In some cases, there is a more restricted mandate to a certain sector of society. More recent developments have included the creation of specialized [children's ombudsmen](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_ombudsmen "Children's ombudsmen").

In some countries, an [inspector general](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspector_general "Inspector general"), citizen advocate or other official may have duties similar to those of a national ombudsman and may also be appointed by a legislature. Below the national level, an ombudsman may be appointed by a state, local, or municipal government. Private ombudsmen may be appointed by, or even work for, a corporation such as a utility supplier, newspaper, [NGO](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NGO "NGO"), or professional regulatory body.

In some jurisdictions, an ombudsman charged with handling concerns about national government is more formally referred to as the "parliamentary commissioner" (e.g. the United Kingdom [Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Commissioner_for_Administration "Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration"), and the [Western Australian state Ombudsman](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ombudsmen_in_Australia#Ombudsman_Western_Australia "Ombudsmen in Australia")). In many countries where the ombudsman's responsibility includes protecting human rights, the ombudsman is recognized as the [national human rights institution](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_human_rights_institutions "National human rights institutions"). The post of ombudsman had by the end of the 20th century been instituted by most governments and by some intergovernmental organizations such as the [European Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union"). As of 2005, including national and sub-national levels, a total of 129 offices of ombudsman have been established around the world.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

The [Roman tribune](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribune "Tribune") had some similar roles, with the power to veto acts that infringed upon the [Plebeians](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plebs "Plebs"). Like other socialist economies that have undertaken economic reforms, such as [post-Soviet Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc "Eastern Bloc") and [Central Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asia "Central Asia"), [reform-era China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_China_(1976%E2%80%931989) "History of China (1976–1989)") has experienced increasing levels of corruption.[[1]](#cite_note-yan2-1)

Public surveys on the mainland since the late 1980s have shown that corruption is among the top concerns of the general public. According to Yan Sun, Associate Professor of Political Science at the [City University of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_University_of_New_York "City University of New York"), it was cadre corruption, rather than a demand for democracy as such, that lay at the root of the social dissatisfaction that led to the [1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre "1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre").[[1]](#cite_note-yan2-1) Corruption undermines the legitimacy of the authoritarian [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) government, adds to [economic inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_inequality "Economic inequality"), undermines the environment, and fuels social unrest.[[2]](#cite_note-pei2007-2)

Since the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre, corruption has not slowed as a result of greater [economic freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_freedom "Economic freedom"), but instead has grown more entrenched and severe in its character and scope. In popular perception, there are more dishonest CCP officials than honest ones, a reversal of the views held in the first decade of the [reform and opening up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_and_opening_up "Reform and opening up") period of the 1980s.[[1]](#cite_note-yan2-1) Chinese political scientist [Minxin Pei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minxin_Pei "Minxin Pei") argued in 2007 that failure to contain widespread corruption is among the most serious threats to China's future economic and political stability.[[2]](#cite_note-pei2007-2) He estimated that year that bribery, kickbacks, theft, and the waste of public funds cost at least three percent of GDP.

The **Politburo of the Chinese Communist Party**, officially the **Political Bureau of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China**, is the [executive committee](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politburo "Politburo") of the [Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party"). Currently, the bureau is a group of 23 top officials who oversee the party and central government. The politburo is headed by the [general secretary](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party"). Unlike the [politburos](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politburo "Politburo") of other [communist parties](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_party "Communist party"), the CCP Politburo subdelegates many of its powers to the smaller [Politburo Standing Committee](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politburo_Standing_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party").

The Politburo is elected by the Central Committee. In practice, however, scholars of Chinese elite politics believe that the Politburo is a self-perpetuating body, with new members of both the Politburo and its Standing Committee chosen through a series of deliberations by current Politburo members and retired Politburo Standing Committee members. # Lens 3B.4 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler build systems for due process, complaint handling, civilian oversight, and independent investigation of abuse, including abuse by politically protected actors?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **strongly negative** — Xi did not build new systems for due process, complaint handling, civilian oversight, or independent investigation of abuse. The 2023 Counterespionage Law, Religious Activity Venues Measures, and Patriotic Education Law expanded state authority over civilians without independent oversight. The Qiqihar school-gym collapse, the Beijing hospital fire, the Yinchuan gas explosion, the Alxa mine collapse, the Jishishan earthquake, and the retiree protests received no independent national inquiry and no personal Xi apology. The PLARF leadership purge and defense-minister removal used a loyalty-first discipline framing without transparent court proceedings.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — 2023 legal-instrument expansion without independent oversight (3B.4 negative)

### 1. Counterespionage Law (April 2023, effective July 2023) — no independent oversight

- **Claim A1.** The NPC Standing Committee passed a revised Counterespionage Law in April 2023, effective July 2023. The revised law restricts the transmission of information related to national security in non-defined terms, allows authorities to inspect electronic equipment and data, and was followed by the Ministry of State Security calling on citizens to engage in counterespionage activity. This expands state authority over civilians without independent oversight, civilian complaint mechanism, or independent investigation appeal.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 ("The revised Counterespionage Law gained the NPC standing committee's approval in April 2023 and took effect in July. The revised law restricts the transmission of information related to national security, which is not clearly defined; it also allows authorities to inspect electronic equipment and data. After the law took effect, the Ministry of State Security called on ordinary citizens to engage in counterespionage activity").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (strongly negative — expanded state authority without independent oversight), 3B.1, 1B.9, 8F.1.

### 2. Religious Activity Venues Measures (effective September 2023) — no independent religious-freedom oversight

- **Claim A2.** The Measures on the Administration of Religious Activity Venues came into force in September 2023, requiring religious venues to indoctrinate followers in CCP ideology, prohibiting "conflict between sects," and barring non-state-approved funding. This expands state authority over religious practice without independent religious-freedom oversight or complaint mechanism.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("The Measures on the Administration of Religious Activity Venues came into force in September. They impose further restrictions on religious activities, requiring religious venues to indoctrinate followers in Chinese Communist Party ideology, and prohibiting them from 'creating conflicts … between sects' or receiving funding other than those approved by the state").
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 (corroborating the May 2023 Najiaying Mosque protest).
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (negative — religious-freedom oversight absent), 3B.1, 8D.4.

### 3. Patriotic Education Law (signed 24 October 2023) — no independent educational-content oversight

- **Claim A3.** On 24 October 2023, Xi signed the Patriotic Education Law (effective 1 January 2024) mandating patriotic education across all levels of schooling, museums, libraries, and tourist sites; requiring internet platforms to produce "patriotic" content; and explicitly extending to Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan, and overseas Chinese. Article 33 mandates internet platforms to develop "new technologies and products to vividly carry out patriotic education." This expands state authority over civilian education without independent educational-content oversight.
  - **Source:** "Patriotic Education Law of the People's Republic of China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriotic_Education_Law_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China ("signed by President Xi Jinping in the same day … came into effect on 1 January 2024 … the main contents of patriotism are: 1. Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Xi Jinping Thought … Article 22 mandates that the law applies to the residents of Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan, and overseas Chinese").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (negative — educational-content oversight absent), 3B.1, 2B.3.

---

## B. Claim-level findings — 2023 industrial-disaster and protest cases with no independent inquiry (3B.4 negative)

### 4. No independent national inquiry into 2023 Qiqihar school-gymnasium collapse (11 dead, 23 July 2023)

- **Claim B4.** On 23 July 2023, the roof of a school gymnasium at No 34 Middle School in Qiqihar, Heilongjiang, collapsed, killing 11 (mostly school volleyball team members) and injuring 4. The direct cause was overloading from improperly placed perlite on the roof. There is no record of an independent national investigation or public correction of the official narrative. Qiqihar officials apologized.
  - **Source:** "2023 Qiqihar school gymnasium collapse" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Qiqihar_school_gymnasium_collapse ("Local police have detained those involved in the adjacent construction project for further investigation … Managers of the involved construction firm are said to face criminal charges. Officials of Qiqihar apologised to the public over the accident").
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (23 July 2023 entry).
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (strongly negative — no independent inquiry, no Xi apology), 3B.1, 3B.2, 8A.

### 5. No independent national inquiry into 2023 Beijing Changfeng Hospital fire (29 dead, 18 April 2023)

- **Claim B5.** On 18 April 2023, a hospital fire at Changfeng Hospital in Beijing's Fengtai District killed 29 and injured 39. CCP Politburo member and Beijing Party Secretary Yin Li visited the site. Police detained twelve people including the hospital director and deputy director. There is no record of a Xi personal apology, an independent national investigation, or public correction of the official narrative.
  - **Source:** "2023 Beijing hospital fire" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Beijing_hospital_fire ("CCP Politburo member and Party Secretary of Beijing Yin Li visited the site and stated that authorities would pursue whoever started the fire … Police detained twelve people, including the hospital's director and deputy director, and the head of the firm overseeing the renovation").
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (19 April 2023 entry).
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (strongly negative — no independent inquiry), 3B.1, 3B.2, 8A.

### 6. No independent national inquiry into 2023 Yinchuan gas explosion (31 dead, 21 June 2023)

- **Claim B6.** On 21 June 2023, a gas explosion at the Fuyang Barbecue Restaurant in Yinchuan, Ningxia, killed 31 and injured seven, caused by a leak in a liquefied-gas tank inside the restaurant. There is no record of a Xi personal apology or public correction of the official narrative.
  - **Source:** "2023 Yinchuan gas explosion" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Yinchuan_gas_explosion ("General Secretary of the Communist Party Xi Jinping urged for utmost efforts in providing medical care to the injured. He ordered an 'all-out rescue and treatment of the injured' and requested strengthened safety measures").
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (21 June 2023 entry).
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (strongly negative — no independent inquiry), 3B.1, 3B.2, 8A.

### 7. No independent national inquiry into 2023 Alxa mine collapse (53 dead, 22 February 2023)

- **Claim B7.** On 22 February 2023, a coal-mine collapse in Alxa Left Banner, Inner Mongolia, killed 53. There is no record of a Xi personal apology, an independent national investigation, or public correction of the official narrative.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (22 February 2023 entry: "53 people are killed by a collapse at a coal mine in Alxa League, Inner Mongolia").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (strongly negative — no independent inquiry), 3B.1, 3B.2, 8A.

### 8. No independent national inquiry into 2023 Jishishan earthquake (151 dead, 18 December 2023)

- **Claim B8.** On 18 December 2023, a magnitude 6.2 earthquake in Jishishan County, Gansu, killed 151 and injured 982 — China's deadliest earthquake in years. There is no record of a Xi personal apology, an independent national investigation, or public correction of the official narrative.
  - **Source:** "2023 Jishishan earthquake" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Jishishan_earthquake ("It caused 151 deaths and 982 injuries to others. This made it China's deadliest earthquake since the 2014 Ludian earthquake").
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (18 December 2023 entry).
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (strongly negative — no independent inquiry), 3B.1, 3B.2, 8A.

### 9. No independent national inquiry into 2023 Typhoon Doksuri flooding deaths (80+ killed, August 2023)

- **Claim B9.** In August 2023, Typhoon Doksuri brought heavy rainfall to Beijing and Hebei, with at least 80 people killed and 35 missing. There is no record of a Xi personal apology for the disaster response, an independent national investigation, or public correction of the official narrative.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (2 August 2023 entry: "At least 80 people are killed and 35 missing by flooding in localities of Beijing, Hebei, Jilin and Liaoning").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (strongly negative — no independent inquiry), 3B.1, 3B.2, 8A.

### 10. No independent response to February 2023 retiree protests in Dalian and Wuhan

- **Claim B10.** In February 2023, several hundred retirees demonstrated in the cities of Dalian and Wuhan against cuts to their medical insurance. There is no record of a Xi personal response to the protest or to the underlying policy. The Counterespionage Law (April–July 2023) and the Religious Activity Venues Measures (September 2023) restricted information transmission about grievances.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 ("Retirees objecting to health-care changes held several large protests in early 2023. In February, for example, several hundred retirees demonstrated in the cities of Dalian and Wuhan").
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("Authorities released on bail some protesters who took part in the White Paper protests in late 2022, including Cao Zhixin, Li Yuanjing, Zhai Dengrui, and Li Siqi").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (strongly negative — no complaint-handling response), 3B.1, 8D.

---

## C. Claim-level findings — 2023 PLARF leadership purge and defense-minister removal used loyalty-first discipline without transparent court proceedings (3B.4 negative)

### 11. 2023 PLARF leadership purge used loyalty-first discipline framing without transparent court proceedings

- **Claim C11.** Between July and October 2023, the entire top of China's nuclear-rocket force was rotated simultaneously: PLARF commander Li Yuchao and deputy commander Liu Guangbin removed; political commissar replaced; replacements Wang Houbin (Navy) and Xu Xisheng (Air Force political work) brought in from outside the branch — "extremely rare" per SCMP. Defense Minister Li Shangfu disappeared in August and was removed 24 October. The CMC's anti-corruption framing of these changes prioritized loyalty over nuclear-strategic competence, and the SCMP/Wikipedia flagged explicit concerns about "the security, credibility and integrity of the PLA." No transparent public court proceedings; no independent oversight; no civilian-led investigation.
  - **Source:** "China names General Wang Houbin …," *South China Morning Post*, 31 July 2023 — https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3229515-china-unveils-new-pla-rocket-force-leadership-after-former-commanders-snared-corruption-scandal ("It is extremely rare for President Xi Jinping, the head of the CMC, to replace a fighting force's commander and its political chief at the same time").
  - **Source:** "People's Liberation Army Rocket Force" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Rocket_Force ("it was thought to be an odd decision to replace the Rocket Force commander with military personnel from outside the branch, and this led to concerns about the security, credibility and integrity of the PLA").
  - **Source:** "Li Shangfu" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Shangfu ("In August 2023, Li disappeared from public view and was then removed from office on October 24, 2023. He is both the shortest-serving Minister of National Defense and the first from the PLA Strategic Support Force … expelled from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) following corruption charges").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (strongly negative — loyalty-first discipline, no transparent court proceedings, no civilian oversight), 1B.3, 1B.7, 8A.4, 8C.1.

### 12. The 2023 anti-corruption campaign was directed at Xi's personal loyalists, not at independent oversight of politically protected actors

- **Claim C12.** The 2023 PLARF leadership purge and defense-minister removal were framed in "serious violation of discipline and law" (NPC Gazette language) without transparent public court proceedings. The anti-corruption campaign was directed against Xi's perceived rivals within the security apparatus (loyalty filter), not against politically protected actors like former Politburo Standing Committee members or against the senior civilian / private-sector network. There is no record of an independent National Supervisory Commission investigation of politically protected actors in 2023.
  - **Source:** "Anti-corruption campaign under Xi Jinping" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-corruption_campaign_under_Xi_Jinping ("the campaign has also led to strengthening of the CCDI apparatus within the CCP, as well as enhanced power over local Discipline Inspection Commissions … [anti-corruption punishment] to officials at or above the vice ministerial level need approval from Xi").
  - **Source:** "Li Shangfu" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Shangfu (cites the NPC Gazette: "serious violation of discipline and law").
  - **Source:** "Li Yuchao" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Yuchao (cites NPCSC bulletin).
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (strongly negative — anti-corruption directed at Xi's rivals, not at independent oversight of politically protected actors), 1B.3, 1B.7, 8A.4, 8C.1.

### 13. The National Supervisory Commission (NSC) — operates as the CCDI's state arm, not as an independent civilian-oversight body

- **Claim C13.** The National Supervisory Commission, formed 2018, is co-located with the CCP's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), the party's supreme supervisory body, and "the NSC effectively functions as the CCDI's state arm." This is the structural design: 2023 had no independent civilian-oversight body.
  - **Source:** "National Supervisory Commission of the People's Republic of China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Supervision_Commission_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China ("The National Supervisory Commission is co-located with the CCP's CCDI, the party's supreme supervisory and disciplinary body, and the NSC effectively functions as the CCDI's state arm").
  - **Source:** "Central Commission for Discipline Inspection" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection ("Safeguarding the political position of Xi and the Central Committee is, officially, the CCDI's highest responsibility").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.4 (strongly negative — no independent civilian oversight; CCDI/NSC under Xi control), 1B.3, 1B.7, 8A.4.

## D. Claim-level findings — 2023 political-prisoner pattern with no transparent process or civilian oversight (3B.4 negative)

### 14. 2023 political-imprisonment campaign against human-rights lawyers with closed-door trials

- **Claim D14.** In 2023, multiple human-rights lawyers were given long sentences in closed-door trials: Xu Zhiyong 14 years (10 April 2023), Ding Jiaxi 12 years (2022, upheld in 2023), Guo Feixiong 8 years (11 May 2023), Yang Shaozheng 4.5 years (August 2023), Qin Yongpei 5 years (March 2023); Yu Wensheng and Xu Yan arrested in April 2023. - **Claim D15.** Rahile Dawut, a Uyghur anthropologist disappeared in December 2017, was sentenced to life imprisonment on "splittism" charges in a secret 2018 trial. ### 16. 2023 Hong Kong NSL trial (47 defendants) with no independent due process

- **Claim D16.** The Hong Kong 47 NSL trial lasted from 6 February to 4 December 2023, with verdicts and sentences of 4 years 2 months to 10 years for 45 of the 47 defendants. Foreign journalists and diplomats were denied entry to the courtroom. The NSL prosecution rate was ~100%.
  - **Source:** "Hong Kong 47" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_47 ("The trial lasted from 6 February to 4 December 2023 … 45 jailed (31 pleaded guilty, 14 found guilty) … Imprisonment of 4 years 2 months to 10 years").

- **Claim D17.** In 2023, journalist-in-exile Yang Zewei was disappeared from his home in Laos in May and reappeared in detention in Hunan province, China. Peng Lifa (Bridge Man protester of 13 October 2022) remained in secret detention as of October 2023, with his family under constant government surveillance and his wife Han Yang and two daughters' personal cell phones confiscated and replaced with government-issued phones.

- **The 2023 PLARF leadership purge and defense-minister removal** used a loyalty-first discipline framing without transparent court proceedings or civilian-led investigation.
- **The 2023 political-imprisonment campaign** (Xu Zhiyong, Ding Jiaxi, Guo Feixiong, Yang Shaozheng, Qin Yongpei, Yu Wensheng, Xu Yan, Rahile Dawut, the Hong Kong 47) used closed-door trials, secret trials, and unverified allegations; the families of the disappeared have no public-process recourse.
